body:
**Specific cigar-butt and special-situation trades**
- **Sanborn Map (1958–60):** about **25% of partnership assets** went into Sanborn in late 1958. The map business's after-tax profits had fallen from over $500,000/yr in the late 1930s to under $100,000 in 1958–59, but the company's investment portfolio was worth more than its share price. Buffett got a board seat and forced the value out [SECONDARY, from the 1960 letter] — [GuruFocus 1960 letter](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/7227/warren-buffett-partnership-letter-of-1960); [MOI Global / Ground Rules](https://moiglobal.com/warren-buffetts-ground-rules/)
- **Dempster Mill (1956–63):** built gradually from an undervalued-security position to control. The partnership owned 70% and associates another 10%. At end-1961, book value was about $75/share and Buffett carried it at $35. He brought in Harry Bottle to liquidate inventory and turn the business around, and the operating assets were sold in 1963. The deal caused local backlash in Beatrice, Nebraska — [MOI Global](https://moiglobal.com/warren-buffetts-ground-rules/); [Hedge Fund Alpha, Dempster](https://hedgefundalpha.com/strategies/warren-buffett-charlie-munger-dempster-mill/)
- **Rockwood & Co. (cocoa arbitrage, 1954, Graham-Newman era):** Jay Pritzker's Rockwood offered $36 of cocoa beans per share while the shares traded at $34. Buffett bought 222 shares himself, and per Miller he skipped the arbitrage and held. The stock reached about $85, for roughly $13,000 of gain vs. about $444 from the arb [SECONDARY, single source; paywalled] — [MOI Global](https://moiglobal.com/warren-buffetts-ground-rules/)
- **American Express, salad-oil scandal (1963–64):** Buffett checked whether customers still used Amex cards and traveler's checks at Ross's Steak House and other Omaha businesses, and through a broker friend, Henry Brandt, polled bank tellers, restaurants and cardholders. He found usage unaffected. Accounts say the partnership built a stake of about **$13M, about 40% of partnership assets**, and exited around 1968 for about $33M. Purchase price is reported variously at $35–41 [SECONDARY; the 40% figure comes from a few sources and I did not verify it against the BPL letters]. Buffett's 1965 letter is often paraphrased as saying he would go to 40% of net worth in a single security under conditions of extremely high probability; I could not fetch the primary text — [The Grain Desk](https://thegraindesk.substack.com/p/main-street-still-trusted-the-card); [The Value Investor](https://www.thevalueinvestor.org/p/warren-buffett-s-investment-in-american-express-a-case-study-in-conviction-investing); [Fortune 2012](https://fortune.com/2012/11/21/why-warren-buffetts-betting-big-on-american-express/amp)
title: buffett_lynch › Cited Findings

body:
- Housel: about 99% of Buffett's net worth was accumulated after age 65. His book cited $81.5bn earned after 65 and $84.2bn after 50. — [CNBC 2024](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/05/03/most-of-warren-buffetts-wealth-came-after-age-65-heres-why.html); [CSQ / Housel](https://csq.com/2020/08/how-warren-buffet-amassed-his-fortune/). Creative Planning (2025) puts it at about 98% after 65. — [Benzinga](https://feeds2.benzinga.com/general/market-summary/25/05/45399940/warren-buffett-shows-how-patience-pays-98-of-his-160-billion-wealth-came-after-turning-65-)
- Housel's counterfactual: if Buffett had started at 30 with $25,000, earned 22% a year, and stopped at 60, he would have about $11.9m, roughly 99.9% less than his actual fortune. — [CSQ / Housel](https://csq.com/2020/08/how-warren-buffet-amassed-his-fortune/); [Irish Times 2025](https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2025/11/15/going-quiet-at-95-buffett-shows-why-time-beats-returns)
- Ronald Read: a Vermont gas-station attendant and JCPenney janitor who died in 2014 at 92 with about $8m. He held dividend stocks in companies he understood and left about $6m to the local hospital and library (the split varies by source). — [CNBC 2016](https://www.cnbc.com/amp/2016/08/29/janitor-secretly-amassed-an-8-million-fortune.html); [AJC](https://www.ajc.com/news/weird-news/who-was-ronald-read-the-janitor-who-amassed-million-fortune-and-gave-all-away/unEhOIxXLh7f66bOtHyFbI)
- Grace Groner: an Abbott Labs secretary who bought 3 shares for $180 in 1935, reinvested the dividends, and died in 2010 at 100 with about $7.2m, which went to Lake Forest College. — [Business Insider NL](https://businessinsider.nl/a-secretary-turned-180-into-7-2-million-by-holding-her-employers-stock-for-75-years/); [Wikipedia: Grace Groner](https://en.Wikipedia.com/wiki/Grace_Groner). Note the survivorship: she held a single employer stock that happened to compound. Many single-stock employee holders (Enron and others) were wiped out.

`insight:investor-edge-taxonomy` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: global, india, process, base-rate, luck-vs-skill

Across this library, edges fall into two buckets. Structural (not copyable): scale and leverage across asset classes (Soros, Druckenmiller), proprietary data/compute/scientists and capacity caps (Simons' Medallion: 39% net 1988-2018, while Renaissance's public funds did far worse), activism and board influence (Ackman), locked-up distressed capital (Marks, Klarman), pre-IPO/block access and network (Indian superstars). Process (largely copyable): Kelly-style sizing (Thorp), downside-first margin of safety (Klarman), special situations driven by non-economic selling (Greenblatt), three-legged stool / scale-economies-shared quality tests (Akre, Sleep, Smith), capital-cycle supply analysis (Andrade), valuation-based allocation (Naren, Jain), avoid-lists and loser-cutting (Arora), scuttlebutt (Fisher), inversion and bias checklists (Munger), cycle temperature (Marks, Templeton). Small size is the individual's one structural advantage: positions in micro/small caps and special situations too small for funds (Greenblatt and Buffett both credit small size early). Common failures across greats: concentration in a broken thesis (Valeant, Horsehead), buying a mania late (Druckenmiller 2000), style droughts of 5+ years (Fundsmith 2021-25, Baupost post-2014, Jain 2018-20). Implication: copy processes, accept multi-year underperformance as normal, and never copy leverage.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| structural | scale, leverage, data, activism, locked capital, deal access |
| process | sizing, MoS, special sits, quality tests, capital cycle, allocation, avoid lists, scuttlebutt, inversion, temperature |

Links: insight:luck-vs-skill (about); insight:winners-drawdowns (about); decision:edge-before-stocks (about)

`insight:marks-on-bubble-watch-2025` | confidence: single-source | date: 2025-01-02

Memo of 2 Jan 2025 (25 years after bubble.com). Cites a J.P. Morgan Asset Management chart of ~324 monthly observations (1988-late 2014) of S&P 500 forward P/E vs subsequent ten-year annualised return: 'There's a strong relationship between starting valuations and subsequent annualized ten-year returns. Higher starting valuations consistently lead to lower returns, and vice versa'; 'when people bought the S&P at p/e ratios in line with today's multiple of 22, they always earned ten-year returns between plus 2% and minus 2%.' Notes banks projecting low- to mid-single-digit ten-year S&P returns; 'the return on an investment is significantly a function of the price paid for it.' Flags concentration: the top-7 stocks' share of the index was roughly 22% in 2000 vs ~one-third now. Not a call to sell everything - he did not say a bubble existed, only that 'investors clearly shouldn't be indifferent to today's market valuation.' Actionable: build an Indian equivalent - Nifty 50 trailing/forward P/E vs subsequent 5/10-yr CAGR (data from NSE index factsheets) - and use starting valuation to set return expectations, not to time exits. Small sample caveat: overlapping 10-yr windows over ~27 years.

Sources:
- https://www.oaktreecapital.com/insights/memo/on-bubble-watch

They are **not recommendations** — no call says or implies buy/sell. Each is scored with Brier score against
a naive base-rate forecaster when it resolves (Jan–Jun 2027). Seed file: `memdb/seeds/2026-11-21_paper_calls_batch2.json`.

**Inputs:** close **₹127.53** on 23-Nov-2026 (NSE bhavcopy = Yahoo; screener 25-Nov ₹126); 10 FY-end P/Es FY17–26 (median **23.9**);
peers 29.9 / 37.2 / 170 (median 37.2); 6-month ADV ₹8.7 cr mean; net debt ₹911 cr (XBRL = deck); base = **core** TTM (EBIT 145.2, EPS 3.51),
normalised EPS 6.69; tax 35%; post-tax interest −45.8 held flat; ROIIC history 3%.
**Scenarios (written before outputs):** blow-up 8% raw (0.25x); bear 30% (+6% → +5%, NOPAT margin 3.5%, ROIIC 4%, exit 14x); base 47%
(+12% → +8%, 5.5%, 8%, 22x); bull 15% (+14% → +11%, 7.0%, 12%, 28x).
**Outputs:** 5-year multiples bear 0.60x / base 1.89x / bull 3.30x / blow-up 0.25x; **EV 1.59x** (raw = anchored) vs hurdle 1.76x; P(≥2x)
34%, P(≥3x) 14%, P(≤0.5x) 17%, blow-up 8%. Base IRR **7.3%** vs CoE 12.5%.
**Reverse DCF:** no growth path reproduces the price; the base path needs a **year-10 NOPAT margin of 33.4%** (today 3.7%). **The scenario
DCF value per share is negative in every scenario (prob-weighted −₹38)**: at ROIIC 4–12% < CoE 12.5%, growth consumes more cash than it
creates, and the operating value lands below the ₹911 cr of net debt. The DCF-consistent exit P/E is therefore negative (−11.5 / −1.7 /
+3.5). **Reading:** on a strict cost-of-capital view the equity is an option on returns improving; the whole 1.59x EV is the exit-multiple
bet (EV at DCF exits −0.13x; at the own median 1.72x). Bull ROIIC 12% is flagged (>5 pts above history) — the bull case *is* the claim that
the European capital starts earning.
**Temperature:** COOL vs own history (0.78x), COLD vs peers (0.50x) on reported EPS; on core EPS (~36x) it would be WARM vs own history.
